source_text: Nihil enim ita pugnat, quam dicere, omnes, et non omnes. Tu dicis, a figulo Deo omnes fieri in condemnationem; Apostolus dicit, non omnes in condemnationem, nec omnes in honorem; quod in loco suo, quid habeat dignitatis absolvam. In ipsa tamen pronuntiatione sententiae, constat inter vos magnam esse discordiam, nec eumdem esse figulum in condemnationem cuncta fingentem, quem Paulus dicat in honorem alios fabricantem; nec te illi credere, qui a magistro admirabili praedicatur; quoniam tuus figulus omnes in condemnationem fingit, Apostoli figulus plurimos fingit in gloriam.
pass_a_gloss: For nothing so fights, as to say, all, and not all. You say, that by God the potter all are made into condemnation; the Apostle says, not all into condemnation, nor all into honor; which in its own place, what dignity it has I will absolve. In the very pronunciation of the sentence nevertheless, it stands that there is a great discord between you, nor is the same potter fashioning all things into condemnation, whom Paul says fabricating others unto honor; nor do you believe him, who is preached by the admirable teacher; since your potter fashions all into condemnation, the Apostle's potter fashions very many into glory.
pass_b_english: Nothing is more contradictory than saying “all” and “not all”. You say that God the potter makes everyone for condemnation. The apostle says that not everyone is for condemnation and not everyone for honor. I will explain the worth of this statement in its proper place. Even in the wording of the statement, however, there is plainly a great disagreement between you. The potter who shapes everyone for condemnation is not the same as the one Paul says fashions some for honor. You do not believe in the one proclaimed by that admirable teacher, because your potter shapes everyone for condemnation, while the apostle's potter shapes very many for glory (compare Romans 9:21).

choices.why: Paul in Julian's citations; keep Apostle not 'Paul' unless Paulus is written.
